danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 39
paragraphs: Flere titusinder af faldne lå i de mest forskelligartede stillinger og uniformer på markerne og engene, der tilhørte Davydov-familien og kronbønderne — de marker og enge, hvor bønderne i Borodino, Gorki, Sjevardino og Semjonovsk i hundreder af år havde høstet deres afgrøder og græsset deres kvæg. Ved forbindingspladserne var græsset og jorden gennemblødt af blod over et areal på flere morgen. Skarer af sårede og usårede af begge parters tropper, med forskræmte ansigter, slæbte sig tilbage — de første mod Mozjajsk, de sidste mod Valuevo. Andre skarer, udmattede og sultne, drevet af deres officerer, marcherede stadig fremad. Endnu andre holdt deres stillinger og fortsatte med at skyde.

Over hele marken, der om morgenen havde været så muntert smuk med glimtet af bajonetter og røgskyer i morgensolen, lå der nu en dis af fugt og røg og en besynderlig skarp lugt af salpeter og blod. Skyer samlede sig, og regndråber begyndte at falde på de døde og sårede, på de forfærdede, de udmattede og de tøvende. Det var, som om de ville sige: »Nok! Nok, mennesker. Hold op! Besind jer! Hvad gør I?«

For mændene på begge sider, der var slidte op af sult og træthed, begyndte det i lige grad at forekomme tvivlsomt, om de skulle fortsætte med at slå hinanden ihjel; alle ansigter udtrykte tøven, og i hver sjæl rejste sig spørgsmålet: »For hvad, for hvem skal jeg dræbe og lade mig dræbe?... I kan gå og gøre, hvad I vil — jeg gider ikke mere!« Denne tanke modnede hen på eftermiddagen i alles sind. Hvert øjeblik kunne alle disse mænd pludselig have grebet sig til hovedet i rædsel over, hvad de foretog sig, og have taget flugten hvorhen som helst.

Men skønt mændene hen imod slagets slutning følte al rædslen i det, de foretog sig, og skønt de ville have været glade for at holde op, fortsatte en uforståelig, mystisk kraft med at beherske dem, og de bragte stadig ladningerne frem, ladede, sigtede og tændte lunterne, skønt der kun var én artillerist for hver tredje kanon, og skønt de snublede og stønnede af udmattelse. Kanonkuglerne fløj lige så hurtigt og grusomt fra begge sider og sønderrev menneskekød, og det forfærdende arbejde, der ikke udførtes af menneskers vilje, men af Hans vilje, som styrer folkene og verdnerne, fortsatte.

Enhver, der kiggede på den russiske hærs uordnede bagtrop, ville have sagt, at hvis blot franskmændene gjorde endnu en lille indsats, ville den forsvinde; og enhver, der kiggede på den franske hærs bagtrop, ville have sagt, at russerne blot behøvede at gøre endnu en lille indsats, og franskmændene ville gå til grunde. Men hverken franskmænd eller russere gjorde den indsats, og kampens flamme døde langsomt hen.

Russerne gjorde ikke den indsats, for det var ikke dem, der angreb franskmændene. I slagets begyndelse stod de blot og spærrede vejen til Moskva, og det gjorde de stadig ved slagets slutning som i begyndelsen. Men selv om russernes mål havde været at drive franskmændene fra deres stillinger, kunne de ikke have gjort denne sidste indsats, for alle de russiske tropper var slået, der var ikke en eneste del af hæren, der ikke havde lidt i slaget, og russerne holdt blot deres plads og mistede halvdelen af deres styrke.

Franskmændene derimod, med mindet om alle deres sejre gennem femten år, med visheden om Napoleons uovervindelighed, med bevidstheden om at have erobret en del af slagmarken og kun at have mistet en fjerdedel af deres tropper, og at de stadig havde den tyve tusinde mand stærke intakte garde — franskmændene kunne nemt have gjort den indsats. Franskmændene, der angreb den russiske hær med det formål at drive den fra dens stillinger, burde have gjort den indsats, for så længe russerne ligesom ved begyndelsen stadig spærrede vejen til Moskva, var det franske mål ikke nået, og alle anstrengelser og tab havde været forgæves. Men franskmændene gjorde det ikke. Nogle historikere hævder, at Napoleon blot behøvede at have sendt sin intakte Gamle Garde ind, og slaget ville have været vundet. At tale om, hvad der ville være sket, hvis Napoleon havde sendt sin garde ind, er det samme som at tale om, hvad der ville ske, hvis efteråret blev til forår. Det kunne ikke ske, og det skete ikke. Napoleon satte ikke garden ind. Ikke fordi han ikke ville, men fordi det ikke lod sig gøre. Hver general, hver officer, hver soldat i den franske hær vidste det: troppernes mod var sunket så dybt, at det ikke kunne lade sig gøre.

Det var ikke Napoleon alene, der havde oplevet den mareridtsagtige følelse af, at den mægtige arm blev ramt af magtesløshed — nej, alle generaler og soldater i hans hær, hvad enten de havde deltaget i slaget eller ej, følte efter al deres erfaring fra tidligere slag — hvor fjenden efter en tiendedel af en sådan indsats var flygtet — den samme rædsel over den fjende, der efter at have mistet halvdelen af sin styrke stadig stod lige så truende ved slagets slutning som ved dets begyndelse. Den moralske kraft hos den angribende franske hær var opbrugt. Ikke den slags sejr, der afgøres af erobrede klude på stænger kaldet faner, eller af den plads, tropperne stod og står på — men en moralsk sejr, som overbeviser fjenden om modpartens moralske overlegenhed og sin egen afmagt, blev vundet af russerne ved Borodino. De franske angribere var som et rasende dyr, der i selve angrebet har fået sit banesår. De mærkede, at de var ved at gå til grunde, men de kunne lige så lidt standse, som den russiske hær, der havde mistet halvdelen af sin styrke, kunne undgå at vige. Den fart, den franske hær allerede havde på, kunne endnu bære den helt til Moskva. Men dér måtte den uden nogen yderligere indsats fra russernes side forbløde af det banesår, den havde fået ved Borodino. Den umiddelbare følge af slaget ved Borodino var Napoleons hovedløse flugt fra Moskva, hans tilbagetog ad den gamle Smolenskvej, invasionshærens undergang med dens halve million mand og Napoleonsfrankrigs fald. Ved Borodino havde en modstander, der var den stærkeste i ånden, for første gang lagt hånd på det.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 39
paragraphs: Tens of thousands of the slain lay in various positions and uniforms on the fields and meadows belonging to the Davydov family and to the crown serfs — those same fields and meadows where for hundreds of years the peasants of Borodino, Gorki, Shevardino, and Semenovsk had harvested their crops and grazed their cattle. At the dressing stations, the grass and earth were soaked with blood across a space of some three acres. Crowds of men from various units, wounded and unwounded, with frightened faces, dragged themselves back toward Mozhaysk from one army and back to Valuevo from the other. Other groups, exhausted and hungry, pushed forward led by their officers. Still others held their ground and continued to fire.

Over the whole field — previously so gaily beautiful with its glitter of bayonets and cloudlets of smoke in the morning sun — there now spread a mist of dampness and smoke and a strange acid smell of saltpeter and blood. Clouds gathered, and drops of rain began to fall on the dead and wounded, on the frightened, exhausted, and hesitating men, as if to say: "Enough, men! Enough! Stop — think about what you are doing!"

To the men on both sides alike, worn out by hunger and fatigue, it equally began to seem doubtful whether they should keep slaughtering each other; on all faces there was hesitation, and the same question arose in every soul: "For what, for whom, must I kill and be killed? You may go and kill whoever you want, but I don't want to do it anymore!" By evening this thought had ripened in every mind. At any moment these men might have been seized with horror at what they were doing and might have thrown everything aside and run anywhere.

But though toward the end of the battle they all felt the full horror of their actions — though they would have been glad to stop — some incomprehensible, mysterious force continued to control them. They still brought up charges, loaded, aimed, and fired, even though only one artilleryman survived out of every three, and though they stumbled and gasped with fatigue, drenched in sweat, caked in blood and powder. The cannonballs flew just as swiftly and cruelly from both sides, crushing human bodies, and that terrible work continued — not by the will of men but at the will of Him who governs men and worlds.

Anyone looking at the disorganized rear of the Russian army would have said that if the French made just one more small effort, it would collapse completely; and anyone looking at the French rear would have said the Russians needed only one more push to destroy them. But neither the French nor the Russians made that effort, and the flame of battle slowly burned out.

The Russians didn't make that effort because they were not the attackers. At the start of the battle they had stood blocking the road to Moscow, and they were still doing so at the end. But even if the Russians had wanted to drive the French from their positions, they couldn't have made this final push — every part of the Russian army had suffered in the battle. Though still holding their ground, they had lost ONE HALF of their men.

The French, with the memory of fifteen years of victories, with confidence in Napoleon's invincibility, with the knowledge that they had captured part of the battlefield and lost only a quarter of their men, and with their Guards still intact — twenty thousand strong — might easily have made that effort. The French, who had attacked the Russian army to drive it from its position, should have made it, because as long as the Russians continued blocking the road to Moscow, the French objective had not been achieved and all their efforts and losses were wasted. But they did not. Some historians say Napoleon only needed to commit his Old Guard and the battle would have been won. Talking about what would have happened if Napoleon had sent his Guards is like discussing what would happen if autumn turned into spring. It couldn't be. Napoleon didn't hold back his Guards because he didn't want to use them — he held back because it couldn't be done. All the generals, officers, and soldiers in the French army knew it couldn't be done, because the army's flagging spirit would not allow it.

It was not Napoleon alone who had experienced that nightmare feeling of a mighty arm struck powerless; all the generals and soldiers felt the same, whether they had fought in the battle or not. After all their experience of previous battles — when after one-tenth of such effort the enemy had fled — they were seized by a similar terror before an enemy who, after losing HALF his men, stood as threateningly at the end as at the beginning. The moral force of the attacking French army was exhausted. Not the kind of victory measured by captured flags on sticks or possession of ground, but a moral victory — one that convinces the enemy of his opponent's spiritual superiority and of his own impotence — was won by the Russians at Borodino. The French invaders, like an infuriated animal that has received a mortal wound in its charge, felt they were dying but could not stop, just as the Russian army, weakened by half, could not help giving way. By momentum alone the French army could still roll forward to Moscow, but there, without any further effort by the Russians, it would have to perish, bleeding from the mortal wound received at Borodino. The direct consequence of the Battle of Borodino was Napoleon's senseless flight from Moscow, his retreat along the old Smolensk road, the destruction of the invading army of five hundred thousand, and the downfall of Napoleonic France — upon which at Borodino, for the first time, the hand of a spiritually stronger opponent had been laid.
